questions: Did your difficulty walking begin suddenly?
Do you have pain in your back or legs when walking?
Do you feel weakness in both legs?
Do you have numbness or tingling in either leg?
Have you ever had a stroke or spinal cord injury?
Have you recently had surgery or an injury involving your back or legs?
Can you walk normally without the crutches when you are alone?
Do you feel that your legs may give way or that you might fall when you walk?
Are you afraid of falling even when you feel physically strong enough to walk?
Does your walking difficulty vary substantially from one occasion to another?
Can you walk better when distracted or when you think nobody is watching?
Can you walk backward without using the crutches?
Can you stand unsupported for at least 30 seconds?
Were these crutches prescribed by a healthcare professional?
Do you use the crutches because of a specific diagnosed medical condition?
Do you feel dizzy or as though the room is moving when you stand or walk?
Do you feel unsteady because you cannot tell where your feet are in space?
Do you have double vision, blurred vision, or difficulty seeing while walking?
Have you had urinary urgency or incontinence along with any problems with thinking or memory?
Do you have tremor, stiffness, slowness, or difficulty initiating steps?
Do you drink alcohol heavily or take sedatives, sleeping tablets, or other medicines that make you drowsy?
Have you had progressive worsening of your walking over months or years?
Do you believe you are physically unable to walk without the crutches despite normal strength testing?
Do you have painful muscle spasms triggered by sudden movement, touch, noise, or emotional stress?
Is the stiffness predominantly in your trunk, abdomen, or legs and worse when you try to walk?
Do you have an exaggerated startle response to unexpected sounds or touch?
Have you been diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, pernicious anemia, or another autoimmune disorder?
Have you had seizures or episodes of brief, unexplained muscle jerks?
Does alcohol or a benzodiazepine such as diazepam noticeably relieve the stiffness?
orders: Perform a focused neurological examination, including manual muscle testing, deep-tendon reflexes, plantar responses, sensory testing (including proprioception and vibration), coordination, and assessment of gait with and without crutches.
Perform a Romberg test and observe whether the patient can rise from a chair and stand unsupported.
Perform the Hoover sign test for functional leg weakness.
Observe the patient rising from a standard chair without using his arms and walking 10 metres without crutches, including turning and walking backward.
Observe the patient’s gait while performing a dual task, such as counting backward by sevens.

Perform a formal movement-disorders examination for parkinsonism, including assessment of resting, postural, and kinetic tremor; rigidity; bradykinesia with finger tapping and toe tapping; facial expression; arm swing; postural stability; and pull test.
Obtain an MRI of the brain, including the posterior fossa, basal ganglia, and ventricular system.
Obtain serum vitamin B1 (thiamine), vitamin B12, folate, TSH, liver function tests, and blood alcohol level.
Perform EMG of paraspinal and lower-limb muscles at rest, assessing for continuous involuntary motor-unit activity and abnormal co-contraction.
Test serum and CSF for anti-GAD65 antibodies, anti-amphiphysin antibodies, and glycine-receptor (GlyR) antibodies.
Perform a lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, and intrathecal anti-GAD65 antibodies.
served: deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses
MRC power in all four limbs
gait with a distracting or automatic task (dancing, counting backwards)
observation for excessive slowness or uneconomic posture
needle EMG (continuous motor unit activity at rest)
neuronal surface / paraneoplastic antibody panel (amphiphysin, glycine receptor, DPPX)
CSF oligoclonal bands and IgG index
lumbar puncture / CSF (cells, protein, oligoclonal bands)
